title: The teachers you met
hook: Marcus, Rumi, Epictetus, Zhuangzi, Julian, the Kotzker Rebbe

segments.voice: Yesterday: the practices you kept. Your line was what survived. Which two did you choose, and did both happen today, even small? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

A Roman emperor's private notebook doesn't open with a plan or a law. Its first book is a list of debts. From my grandfather, good morals and an even temper. From my mother, generosity, and a simple way of living. From my tutor, not to take sides at the chariot races, and to put up with hard work and want little. Name after name. Before the book turns to his own thoughts, Marcus Aurelius sets down where each good thing came from. Today, we do the same: the teachers you met.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S PRIVATE NOTEBOOK.` → `BOOK ONE: A LIST OF DEBTS.` → `WHERE EACH GOOD THING CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Let's walk the line of them, one at a time, each in their own house. First, the Stoics. Marcus, arguing with himself under the blankets, in the notebook known by its Greek title, to himself. Epictetus, who was enslaved, and who, the story goes, warned his master he'd break his leg and, when it broke, said only: didn't I tell you? He taught that some things are in our power and some aren't. Second, the mystics of the heart. Rumi, the Persian poet whose Masnavi opens with a reed flute crying for the reed bed it was cut from, a song some readers hear as the soul missing home. And Julian of Norwich, an English anchoress, who in a vision saw all that is made as small as a hazelnut in her palm, and wrote down what she was shown. In Grace Warrack's translation: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tricksters of the way. Zhuangzi, the Chinese sage who dreamed he was a butterfly and woke unsure which one was dreaming. Fourth, the fierce ones. The Kotzker Rebbe, a Hasidic master in nineteenth-century Poland, remembered for his impatience with anything fake. Asked where God lives, the story goes, he answered: wherever people let God in. They never met, and they wouldn't have agreed on everything. That's why we left each in their own house. But every one of them handed you something, the way Marcus's teachers handed him an even temper. Naming it is the thank-you.
screen: `MARCUS AND EPICTETUS.` · `RUMI AND JULIAN.` · `ZHUANGZI AND THE BUTTERFLY.` · `THE KOTZKER: LET IT IN.` · then, large: `THANK THE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Pick one teacher from this year. One of these, or another you met along the way. Now finish Marcus's sentence for yourself, silently: from this teacher, I learned. One thing. Keep it simple, the way he did. Then, if you like, write it down as a short thank-you note, to someone who can't read it. You're naming where it came from. The bell holds the time.
The teachers you met. Marcus, Epictetus, Rumi, Julian, Zhuangzi, the Kotzker Rebbe: each in their own house, each handing you something. Today's word.
Your line: thank the teachers. Write one line today, the way Marcus did: from this person, I learned this. A living teacher counts too. Maybe tell them. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 328 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOU STILL DON'T KNOW.`

howItsDone: Many traditions honor their teachers by name, reciting lineages or remembering them on set days; Marcus Aurelius opened his Meditations with a list of what he learned from each person who shaped him.

notes: Meditations I: grandfather Verus (good morals, government of temper), mother (piety, beneficence, simplicity of living), tutor (not to be a partisan of the Green or Blue at the races; to endure labor, want little). Paraphrased; confirm the hook's order and wording.
Julian, Warrack 1901, ch. 27 (Thirteenth Revelation): confirm exact wording.
Kotzker 'wherever people let God in' is an oral Hasidic tradition (told on day 63); 'the story goes' used.
Pronunciation of τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν given in a simplified Erasmian style; a classicist may adjust.
Epictetus's leg story (day 23) comes from Celsus via Origen; script now says 'the story goes'.

Editor review 2026-10-01: rewrote the hook to drop 'nearly two thousand years ago', 'the most powerful man in the world' and 'the first thing he wrote' (the order of composition is unknown; only the book order is certain), and fixed the attribution: in Meditations I.5 the races and 'endure labour, want little' both come from the same tutor (governor), not two teachers. Softened 'the song of every soul' to 'some readers hear', dropped the unsourced 'single room attached to a church' detail and 'famous', cut the joy-of-fish clause (day 329 uses it) and replaced the myth item that repeated day 319's Marcus Book I item.
